newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour calls off talks on TV election debate.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour calls off talks on TV election debate.

text.p: Britain's main opposition Labour Party on Thursday called off talks with the ruling Conservatives on a televised debate between the party leaders ahead of the May 1 general election.
The announcement cast grave doubt on whether the debate, which would be the first of its kind in British electoral history, would ever take place.

Labour's campaign manager Peter Mandelson accused the Conservatives of being "unable to be flexible and to come to a final decision" on the debate between Prime Minister John Major and Labour leader Tony Blair.
"We have decided that the present negotiations must be treated as at an end," Mandelson said in statement.

Labour, however, remained committed to the idea of a debate and was exploring other avenues, including the possible involvement of veteran broadcaster and political interviewer Sir David Frost, Mandelson said.

Michael Dobbs, who is heading the Conservatives' team negotiating conditions for the debate, accused Labour of "pulling the plug" on the idea and said it was now up to Mandelson whether there would be a debate at all.

Both Major and Blair have agreed to the debates, but the format has proved a problem, largely because of the need to fulfil election rules guaranteeing all major parties equal air time during the election campaign.
The Scottish National Party on Thursday lost a legal bid to prevent the debate going ahead without its own leader, Alex Salmond, taking part.
Britain's Liberal Democrats have also threatened legal action if their leader, Paddy Ashdown, is not given a role in the head-to-head debate.
